paragraphs.title: The Siege, the Fall of Jerusalem, and Zedekiah’s Fate

answers: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his host
The king of Egypt and his army
easy.explanation: Nebuchadnezzar and all his host came against Jerusalem and built forts around it.
easy.q: Who came against Jerusalem and besieged it?

answers: Until the eleventh year of king Zedekiah
easy.explanation: The city was besieged until the eleventh year of king Zedekiah.

answers: He was brought to the king of Babylon for judgment
easy.explanation: The Chaldees brought Zedekiah to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where judgment was given upon him.
easy.q: What happened to Zedekiah after he was captured?

answers: The famine prevailed, and there was no bread
medium.explanation: The famine prevailed in the city, and there was no bread for the people.
medium.q: What made the situation in Jerusalem especially difficult before the city was broken up?

answers: Through the Temple gate by day
By night through the gate between two walls
medium.explanation: They fled by night through the gate between two walls, near the king’s garden.
medium.q: How did the men of war escape from Jerusalem?

answers: Siege structures built by the besieging army
medium.explanation: Nebuchadnezzar’s army built forts against the city round about as part of the siege.
medium.q: What were the forts built around Jerusalem?

answers: The famine showed the city’s severe distress before it fell
The famine caused the Babylonians to leave
The famine caused Zedekiah to defeat Babylon
challenge.explanation: The famine prevailed before the city was broken up, showing Jerusalem’s weakened condition.
challenge.q: What connection does the passage show between the famine and the fall of Jerusalem?

answers: The king was left without military support
The army joined Zedekiah in victory
challenge.explanation: After the Chaldees overtook Zedekiah, all his army was scattered from him.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that all Zedekiah’s army was scattered from him?

answers: Siege, breaking up of the city, escape, capture, and judgment
Escape, siege, judgment, and then the city’s fall
challenge.explanation: The city was besieged, then broken up; Zedekiah fled, was captured, and was judged.
challenge.q: What is the correct order of events?

paragraphs.title: The Destruction of Jerusalem and the Exile

easy.explanation: Nebuzar-adan, captain of the guard, came to Jerusalem.
easy.q: Who came to Jerusalem in the fifth month?

answers: The house of the LORD, the king’s house, and the houses of Jerusalem
easy.explanation: He burned the Temple, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem.
The army of the Chaldees broke down the walls round about.
easy.q: What did the Chaldees do to the walls of Jerusalem?

answers: The city was devastated and most of the people were carried away
The king returned to rule the city
medium.explanation: Nebuzar-adan carried away the rest of the people and the remnant of the multitude.
medium.q: What was the result of the city being burned and its walls destroyed?

answers: The poor of the land, to be vinedressers and husbandmen
medium.explanation: The captain of the guard left the poor of the land to work as vinedressers and farmers.
medium.q: Who was left in the land?

answers: The ordinary and humble people who remained
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the people of low social status who were left in the land.
medium.q: What does “the poor of the land” mean in this passage?

answers: The destruction was limited to the Temple
The destruction included the religious center, the royal house, and the people’s homes
The destruction affected only the army
challenge.explanation: The passage names the house of the LORD, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem.
challenge.q: What does the movement from burning the LORD’s house to burning the city houses show about the destruction?

answers: To show that some people remained to cultivate the land
challenge.explanation: They describe the work assigned to the people who remained in the land.
challenge.q: Why are the vinedressers and husbandmen mentioned?

answers: He left farmers, burned the city, carried people away, and broke the walls
He burned the city, broke the walls, carried many away, and left ordinary workers
He carried everyone away, rebuilt the walls, and burned the Temple
challenge.explanation: This is the sequence described in verses 8–12.
challenge.q: What is the correct order of Nebuzar-adan’s actions?

paragraphs.title: The Plundering of the Temple Vessels

easy.explanation: The passage mentions bronze vessels, gold things, and silver things.
easy.q: What main materials were taken from the Temple vessels?

answers: They broke them in pieces and carried the brass to Babylon
They left them in the Temple
They made weapons from them in Jerusalem
easy.explanation: They broke the pillars and carried their brass to Babylon.
easy.q: What did the Chaldees do to the pillars of brass?

easy.explanation: The passage says that Solomon had made them for the house of the LORD.
easy.q: Who made the pillars, the sea, and the bases?

medium.explanation: The firepans, bowls, and other vessels of gold and silver were taken.
medium.q: Which of these is listed as a vessel that was taken?

answers: Their weight was small and fixed
The brass of all these vessels was without weight
They were made only of silver
medium.explanation: The brass of all these vessels was without weight, meaning it was immeasurable.
medium.q: What does the passage say about the weight of the brass vessels?

answers: Supports or stands for the Temple furnishings
medium.explanation: The bases were Temple supports or stands, listed with the pillars and the brasen sea.
medium.q: What were the bases mentioned in the passage?

answers: They dismantled the large objects so they could carry them away
They hid the vessels in the Temple
challenge.explanation: The large bronze objects were broken apart before their metal was carried to Babylon.
challenge.q: What is suggested by the statement that the Chaldees “brake in pieces” the vessels?

answers: Their chapiters had wreathen work and pomegranates of brass
They were made of plain wood
They were lower than the city walls
challenge.explanation: The chapiters were decorated with wreathen work and pomegranates.
challenge.q: Which detail emphasizes the ornate appearance of the pillars?

answers: Gold vessels, then the walls, then the pillars
Bronze vessels, gold and silver vessels, and then details about the pillars
The pillars, then Gedaliah’s appointment, then the silver vessels
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from bronze vessels to gold and silver items and then describes the pillars.
challenge.q: What is the correct order in the description of the Temple plunder?

paragraphs.title: The Capture of Jerusalem’s Leaders and Judah’s Exile

easy.explanation: Nebuzar-adan took Seraiah the chief priest.
easy.q: Who was taken as the chief priest?

answers: To Riblah, to the king of Babylon
easy.explanation: They were brought to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
easy.q: Where were the captured leaders brought?

answers: Judah was carried away out of its land
easy.explanation: The passage concludes, “So Judah was carried away out of their land.”
easy.q: What happened to Judah at the end of the passage?

answers: Priests, military officers, officials, scribes, and people of the land
medium.explanation: The list includes priests, keepers of the door, military officers, royal attendants, a scribe, and sixty people.
medium.q: What groups of people were taken from Jerusalem?

medium.explanation: They were brought before the king of Babylon, who smote and slew them at Riblah.
medium.q: Why were the captured people brought to the king of Babylon at Riblah?

answers: He was set over the men of war
medium.explanation: The officer was set over the men of war in the city.
medium.q: What was the officer’s role in this passage?

answers: It affected leadership, the army, officials, and the general population
challenge.explanation: The list includes religious leaders, military leaders, officials, scribes, and people of the land.
challenge.q: What does the variety of people taken from Jerusalem show about the extent of the destruction?

answers: The removal of the leaders was part of Judah’s defeat and exile
The removal of the leaders brought Judah independence
challenge.explanation: The passage describes the leaders being taken and ends by saying Judah was carried away.
challenge.q: What connection is shown between taking the leaders and Judah’s exile?

answers: Sixty people of the land were also taken
Only the chief priest was taken
challenge.explanation: The passage specifically mentions threescore men of the people of the land.
challenge.q: Which detail in the list of captives is easy to overlook?

paragraphs.title: Gedaliah, the Assassination, and the Flight to Egypt

easy.explanation: Nebuchadnezzar made Gedaliah ruler over the people left in Judah.
easy.q: Whom did the king of Babylon make ruler over the remaining people?

easy.explanation: They came to Gedaliah at Mizpah.
easy.q: Where did the captains and their men meet Gedaliah?

easy.explanation: Ishmael came with ten men and smote Gedaliah so that he died.

answers: Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon
Rebel against the king of Babylon
medium.explanation: Gedaliah told them to dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon.
medium.q: What did Gedaliah tell the people to do?

answers: They were afraid of the Chaldees
They wanted to build a Temple
medium.explanation: The people and the army captains went to Egypt because they were afraid of the Chaldees.
medium.q: Why did the people go to Egypt after Gedaliah’s death?

answers: A governor appointed to govern the people
medium.explanation: Gedaliah was appointed by the king of Babylon to govern the remaining people.
medium.q: What did “ruler” mean in Gedaliah’s role?

answers: Gedaliah urged them to remain, but the people fled to Egypt
Gedaliah urged rebellion, but the people stayed
Gedaliah urged them to build walls, and the people built the Temple
challenge.explanation: Gedaliah said it would be well with those who remained, but the people later fled because of fear.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between Gedaliah’s advice and the people’s action after his death?

answers: The attack was organized rather than accidental
He came as the king of Babylon’s representative
challenge.explanation: The passage deliberately notes that Ishmael came with ten men.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from Ishmael arriving with ten men?

answers: The people went to Egypt, Gedaliah was appointed, and Ishmael arrived
Gedaliah was appointed, urged the people to remain, Ishmael killed him, and the people fled
Ishmael killed Gedaliah, and afterward Gedaliah was appointed
challenge.explanation: This is the order given in verses 22–26.
challenge.q: What is the correct sequence of events?

paragraphs.title: Jehoiachin’s Release and a Thread of Hope

easy.explanation: Evil-merodach king of Babylon lifted up Jehoiachin’s head out of prison.

answers: An honored position and food each day
easy.explanation: He set Jehoiachin’s throne above the other kings and gave him a daily allowance.

answers: His prison garments were changed, and he ate before the king
He exchanged them for Egyptian clothing
easy.explanation: The passage says that his prison garments were changed and that he ate bread continually before the king.
easy.q: What happened to Jehoiachin’s clothing after his release?

medium.explanation: The king spoke kindly to Jehoiachin, honored him, and provided for him.
medium.q: What does “lifted up the head of Jehoiachin” mean in this context?

answers: He changed from a prisoner to an honored person among kings
He changed from king to common messenger
He changed from official to prisoner
medium.explanation: He came out of prison and was given an honored position above the thrones of the kings.
medium.q: What change in Jehoiachin’s status is described?

answers: A portion or regular supply of food
medium.explanation: Jehoiachin received a continual daily allowance from the king.
medium.q: What does “allowance” mean in this passage?

answers: It presents release, honor, and provision instead of destruction and exile
It describes another destruction of Jerusalem
It describes the beginning of the siege
challenge.explanation: The final verses focus on Jehoiachin’s release and favorable treatment.
challenge.q: How does the ending differ from the events that came before it?

answers: Renewed recognition of his royal status
The complete loss of his position
His appointment as Babylon’s army commander
challenge.explanation: The honored position suggests that his royal dignity was recognized again.
challenge.q: What might Jehoiachin’s throne being set above the thrones of the kings signify?

answers: He received a daily allowance all the days of his life
He received bronze vessels one time
challenge.explanation: The text says his allowance was continual and given every day for all his life.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that Jehoiachin’s favor continued rather than occurring only once?
